Newborn Care

Fever after birth: when to get medical help

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Fever after giving birth can come from the uterus, a healing wound, the breasts, the urinary tract or another illness. Some causes are readily treatable, but deciding that it is simply part of recovery can delay important care. Report a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher immediately, and seek help sooner if you feel seriously unwell.

A measured fever deserves prompt care

After giving birth, it can be difficult to separate normal recovery from a new illness. Sweating, tiredness and breast fullness can all occur, but a measured temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher is an urgent maternal warning sign. Contact your maternity team or seek medical care immediately. If you cannot reach a clinician promptly, use an urgent or emergency service rather than waiting overnight.

You do not need to identify the cause first. Tell the service when you gave birth, whether you had a vaginal or caesarean birth, your temperature and any other symptoms. Significant illness can occur with a lower or even normal temperature, so feeling rapidly worse also matters. A fever-reducing medicine does not establish that an infection has gone away.

Know which accompanying symptoms are emergencies

Call emergency services for trouble breathing, chest pain, collapse, confusion, a seizure or severe, continuing abdominal pain. Very heavy vaginal bleeding, such as soaking a pad in an hour, or passing very large clots with feeling faint needs urgent assessment. New pain, redness or marked swelling in one leg can indicate a clot and must be assessed promptly.

Do not drive yourself if you feel faint or seriously unwell. Ask someone to stay with you and help with the baby. Take your discharge paperwork and medicine list if readily available, but do not delay departure to collect them. Always mention recent pregnancy, including when seeking care outside the maternity service.

A caesarean wound can become infected

Both planned and unplanned caesarean births leave an incision that needs time to heal. Some discomfort is expected, but increasing pain, spreading redness, swelling, heat, pus or an unpleasant smell needs review. A wound that opens or starts bleeding also requires advice, particularly if you have fever or feel unwell.

A sore incision is not the only possible source of fever after surgery. Deep abdominal pain, painful urination or foul-smelling vaginal discharge may point elsewhere, so describe all symptoms rather than assuming the skin wound explains everything. Follow the dressing and cleaning instructions given by your surgical team; do not squeeze the wound or try to close an opening yourself.

Endometritis is an infection inside the uterus

Postpartum endometritis affects the lining of the uterus. It often begins in the first one to three days after birth, but later symptoms still need attention. Fever or chills, lower-abdominal tenderness, feeling generally ill and unpleasant-smelling discharge are possible signs. Ordinary postpartum bleeding can coexist with infection, so its presence alone does not distinguish normal recovery from illness.

Risk is higher after caesarean birth and can also be increased by prolonged labour, a long interval after the waters break, infection during labour, retained or manually removed placental tissue, diabetes and certain bacteria in the genital tract, including group B streptococci. These are reasons for clinical awareness, not proof that someone will develop an infection.

Give the team the relevant birth history

Mention assisted birth with forceps or vacuum, any infection or unusual fluid during labour, manual placental removal and whether the placenta was thought to be complete. Information about a preterm or overdue birth and gestational diabetes may help the team understand the overall course. None of these details, by itself, establishes the cause of a fever.

If pieces of placenta or other pregnancy tissue remain in the uterus, they can contribute to bleeding and infection. The clinician may arrange imaging or other assessment and decide whether treatment beyond antibiotics is needed. Do not wait for a routine postnatal appointment if pain, fever, unusual discharge or bleeding is worsening.

Mastitis involves inflammation, sometimes with infection

A hot, swollen, painful breast area, a tender lump or wedge-shaped patch can accompany fever, aching, headache and fatigue. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin. Mastitis is inflammation of breast tissue; some cases are bacterial, but inflammation itself can cause systemic symptoms. It can also occur outside breastfeeding and deserves assessment in that situation.

Milk production and breast swelling change rapidly in the early days. Do not assume that a fever must be harmless because milk is coming in, or that it will settle within 24 hours. Tell the clinician about breast symptoms when you report the fever. A persistent painful swelling, worsening illness or failure to improve with treatment may require assessment for an abscess.

Use gentle breast care while following the treatment plan

For most breastfeeding parents with mastitis, continuing normal, responsive feeds is appropriate. If feeding is too painful or milk is not being removed effectively, ask for help with attachment and an expression plan. Avoid forceful massage or repeatedly pumping to empty the breast; these can worsen swelling or oversupply. If you are not breastfeeding but are producing milk, ask how to relieve discomfort without stimulating unnecessary extra production.

A cool pack wrapped in cloth can ease discomfort. Cabbage leaves have not been shown to work better than ice, so they are not an essential treatment. Routine nipple scrubbing or washing before and after every feed is unnecessary; seek help for cracked or painful nipples instead. Hand hygiene and appropriate cleaning of feeding equipment still matter. Breast comfort measures should accompany, not delay, assessment of a postpartum fever.

A urinary infection may affect the bladder or kidneys

Burning when passing urine, an urgent or frequent need to go, passing small amounts, lower-abdominal discomfort or a feeling of incomplete emptying may suggest a urinary problem. Having had a urinary catheter is useful information because catheter use can increase infection risk. A urine sample may help guide treatment.

Urine can sting when it touches a healing tear, but persistent or worsening pain should not automatically be called normal after birth. Fever or chills with back or side pain, nausea or marked illness can indicate a kidney infection and needs urgent care. Being unable to empty the bladder also needs prompt assessment; it is not something to manage simply by forcing more fluid.

Tears, stitches and other illnesses need consideration too

A perineal tear or episiotomy can become infected. Tell the team about increasing soreness, swelling, discharge, a bad smell or a wound that seems to be opening. Inflammation is part of healing, but this does not make a measured fever safe to ignore. The recovery pattern and examination matter more than deciding on your own that the stitches are probably responsible.

People who have just given birth can also develop respiratory, gastrointestinal and other illnesses unrelated to the birth wound. Fever with rapidly worsening weakness or confusion can be part of sepsis, a dangerous response to infection. The team may need to look beyond the first obvious symptom when deciding what tests and treatment you need.

Treatment is chosen for the cause and severity

Assessment may include temperature and other vital signs, examination of the abdomen, wound or breasts, and urine or blood tests. Depending on the findings, imaging or cultures may be needed. Bacterial urinary, uterine, wound or breast infections can require antibiotics. The medicine, route and duration depend on the suspected site, allergy history, local resistance and how unwell you are.

More serious infections may need intravenous antibiotics, fluids and hospital monitoring. An abscess or retained tissue can need a procedure as well. Do not take leftover antibiotics or someone else’s prescription. Tell the prescriber if you are breastfeeding and if your baby was premature or has a medical condition, so the treatment plan considers both of you.

Prevention supports recovery but cannot prevent every infection

Wash your hands before and after wound care, keep the caesarean incision clean and dry as instructed, and change dressings on the schedule your team provides. Clean the perineal area gently with water, change maternity pads regularly and avoid putting products inside the vagina while healing. Sterile water and aggressive washing are not routine requirements for home perineal care.

Do not place witch-hazel pads, herbal products or unprescribed creams on an incision without advice. An infection does not mean you were careless. Some risks arise from the birth or the bacteria normally present in the body and cannot be eliminated by additional washing.

Antibiotics given around a caesarean are a separate preventive decision made by the surgical team. A major 2016 trial found fewer postoperative infections when azithromycin was added to standard antibiotic prophylaxis for unplanned caesarean births. This does not mean everyone should start azithromycin after going home, or use it to treat an unexplained fever.

Relieve discomfort and arrange clear follow-up

Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, and ibuprofen are commonly used after birth and are generally compatible with breastfeeding when appropriate for the individual. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about your health conditions, other medicines and the correct product. Avoid taking several products containing the same ingredient, and follow the prescribed or labelled directions.

Rest, regular drinks if you have no fluid restriction, and help with baby care can support recovery. Before leaving an appointment, ask when improvement should begin, how results will be communicated and who to contact if symptoms continue. Get reassessed promptly if you feel worse, cannot keep fluids or medicines down, or develop a new warning sign. Do not wait to finish an antibiotic course before reporting deterioration.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC identifies a temperature of at least 38°C as an urgent maternal warning sign.

Breastfeeding guidance distinguishes inflammatory mastitis from bacterial infection and discourages aggressive massage or over-pumping.

How BeMama can help

Keep your maternity contact number and a short symptom record together, so another adult can help you seek care.

When to seek help

Seek immediate medical care for postpartum fever; call emergency services for collapse, confusion, breathing difficulty, severe pain or heavy bleeding.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A postpartum fever should not be dismissed as milk coming in or stitches healing.
  • Report abdominal, wound, urinary and breast changes together.
  • Treatment may include antibiotics, drainage or other care depending on the cause.
  • Gentle hygiene supports healing; infection is not a personal failure.
  • Fever medicine does not replace assessment or follow-up.

Frequently asked questions

Can I wait overnight if the temperature is only 38°C?

No. A temperature of 38°C or higher after birth warrants immediate medical advice or assessment, even if you are not sure of the cause.

Does a normal temperature rule out a serious complication?

No. Severe pain, heavy bleeding, collapse, confusion or breathing difficulty needs urgent care regardless of the thermometer reading.

Can milk coming in explain away a fever?

No. Breast fullness can occur during normal recovery, but a measured fever needs assessment rather than a promise that it will settle in 24 hours.

Is every case of mastitis a bacterial infection?

No. Mastitis describes inflammation. Some cases need antibiotics, while others need supportive care and feeding adjustments; your symptoms guide assessment.

Should I stop breastfeeding or pump until the breast is empty?

Most people can continue normal feeds. Repeated emptying and forceful massage may worsen inflammation. Ask for an individual feeding and expression plan.

Is painful urination always normal after a vaginal birth?

No. Healing tissue may sting, but persistent pain, frequent urges, fever or side pain needs review for urinary infection or another problem.

Can uterine infection occur after a vaginal birth?

Yes. Caesarean birth increases risk, but endometritis can occur after either type of birth.

Should I take azithromycin left over at home?

No. Preventive antibiotics around surgery are different from treating a new postpartum fever. The cause and appropriate prescription need assessment.

Do I need sterile water and nipple washing after every feed?

Routine home hygiene does not require sterile water for perineal washing or repeated nipple scrubbing. Follow your discharge and feeding-equipment instructions.

What if antibiotics or fever medicine are not helping?

Contact the care team again. Worsening illness, new symptoms or inability to take treatment needs reassessment; do not wait for the course to end.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
